dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Gold does not occur in one way. Where it sits decides how you look for it, and how you would mine it.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Orogenic lode gold. Quartz and carbonate veins in deformed greenstone belts: steep, narrow, high grade and deep. Most of the gold in Africa and Australia.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Epithermal. Shallow, close to volcanoes, formed where hot spring fluids boil. Veins and stockworks, often carrying silver as well.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Porphyry copper-gold. Enormous and low grade, built around a cooling intrusion, with gold as a by-product of copper. Half a gram a tonne, but a billion tonnes of it.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Volcanogenic massive sulphide. Metal dumped onto an ancient sea floor by black smokers, then folded into the crust.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Laterite. Not a new deposit at all, but an old one weathered in place, with the gold left behind and enriched in the soil.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: And placer. Gold freed by weathering and sorted by moving water. Part six is entirely about those.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Now, grade. Gold grade is grams per tonne, and the numbers are much smaller than people expect.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: This block is one tonne of rock. And this is one gram of gold, drawn at the same scale. Two point three millimetres across.

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Around one gram per tonne is the cut-off for a big open pit. Underground needs three to five. A rich narrow vein might run twenty. And a speck you can actually see in a hand specimen is already an unusually rich rock.

dialogue.speaker: juma
dialogue.text: So how do you know whether a whole deposit is worth anything?

dialogue.speaker: zawadi
dialogue.text: Ten million tonnes at two grams a tonne is twenty million grams. About six hundred thousand ounces. That is a mine. One spectacular rock is a rock.
